title: How the Brain Times Sound to the Microsecond — Without a Stopwatch
hook: Locating a sound relies on timing differences between your ears smaller than a millionth of a second — using neurons that individually react far slower than that. A new model explains how.
key_points: Sound localization depends on interaural time differences (ITDs) as small as a few microseconds.
The classic 1948 Jeffress model assumed the brain uses precise wiring: fixed delay lines feeding coincidence-detector neurons.
A new model shows the same microsecond precision can emerge from a network settling into a stable equilibrium, on much slower neural timescales.
No finely-tuned delay circuitry is required — the population's collective dynamics do the work.
The model still reproduces known physiological patterns, like how 'best' delays vary with sound frequency.
content_html: Your brain can tell that a sound reached your left ear a few millionths of a second before your right — and use that gap to pinpoint where the sound came from. The puzzle is that the neurons doing this respond far more sluggishly than that. A new modeling paper offers an explanation.
extra_html: The textbook explanation, proposed by Jeffress in 1948, imagined the brain wiring up literal delay lines: signals from each ear travel down neural pathways of carefully staggered lengths, and a "coincidence detector" neuron fires when two signals arrive at exactly the same moment — implicitly measuring the time difference. This new work proposes something different: interaural time is instead represented as a stable equilibrium point in the collective activity of a neural population, shaped by excitatory and inhibitory interactions across frequency channels. Despite relying on slow-moving population dynamics rather than exact timing circuitry, the resulting system still locates the equilibrium with microsecond precision, and reproduces real physiological patterns — such as how a neuron's preferred time delay shifts with sound frequency — without needing any finely tuned wiring at all.

related.title: The Senses
related.hook: Light, sound, chemicals, and pressure can't enter your brain directly — your senses translate all of them into the one language your neurons understand: electrical signals.

related.title: Neurons and Signals
related.hook: Your every thought, twitch, and feeling rides on tiny electrical pulses fired by neurons — and leaps the gaps between them as bursts of chemicals.

flashcards.prompt: Why is precise sound localization a puzzle for neuroscience?
flashcards.back_html: It requires sensitivity to timing differences between the ears of just a few microseconds — yet the neurons involved individually respond on much slower, sluggish timescales.

flashcards.prompt: What did the classic 1948 Jeffress model propose to explain this precision?

choices.text: Fixed-length neural 'delay lines' feeding coincidence-detector neurons
A single neuron that directly measures the sound's travel time
The eardrums physically synchronizing before any neural processing

flashcards.explanation_html: Jeffress proposed precise wiring: neurons tuned to detect coincidences after signals traveled along delay lines of different fixed lengths.

flashcards.prompt: What's the key idea in this new alternative model?

choices.text: Microsecond precision emerges from a network settling toward a stable equilibrium, without needing exact delay circuitry
Each ear counts individual sound wave cycles and compares totals
The brain ignores timing and localizes sound purely from loudness

flashcards.explanation_html: Instead of precise wiring, excitatory and inhibitory interactions across the neural population drive a slow dynamical system toward an equilibrium that encodes the estimated time difference — reproducing microsecond precision.
